1.pericope_label: The song of Moses begins: the Lord my strength, and a man of war

schools.summary: Gill notes that this is the first song on record and reports a Jewish reckoning of ten songs beginning with one sung by Adam when his sins were forgiven, together with another saying, not easily squared with it, that from the creation to the standing by the sea no man ever sang a song but Israel; he refers the word for man in the third verse to the future incarnation, since as yet he was not really man. Calvin holds that the song was introduced in confirmation of the history as well as in gratitude, since it was dictated about no unknown event and brought the hearers forward as eye-witnesses, so that later ages might know nothing had been written which had not been openly declared by six hundred thousand men besides their wives and children, and asks to whom they could have lied when they were witnesses to one another and no stranger was listening.

Henry marks the contrast with what went before, that those who had to hold their peace while the deliverance was working must not hold it now that it was wrought, and that the less they had to do then, the more they had to do now.

Clarke points out that the word rendered Lord in the second verse is not the full name but the contracted form, reported on another's authority to stand as if by abbreviation and to signify the Essence, he who is, simply and absolutely and independently; on the third verse he would change the English to make the Lord the hero of the battle, since the received phrase is now scarcely applied to anything but ships of war and the object was to show that man had no part in the victory. Wesley draws a conclusion about worship, that since psalm-singing was used before the ceremonial law was given it is no part of that law and was not abolished with it, singing being as much the language of holy joy as praying is of holy desire.

Ellicott finds it scarcely conceivable that the song had any other author than Moses, since it resembles Egyptian religious poetry with which he and probably no other Israelite of the time would have been familiar, and breathes a tone scarcely shared by any contemporary; he reports that the prophetic statements in the later verses have led some to date it after Joshua and answers that their vagueness contrasts remarkably with the definiteness of the descriptive part. He notes the first appearance of the contracted divine name, its earlier currency in speech as an older place-name shows, and its choice here for the rhythm, observes that a prophet afterwards took the following clause into one of his poems, reports the division of the versions over the clause about preparing a habitation, and praises the translators for keeping the boldness of the anthropomorphism in the third verse while dismissing the ancient softenings as turgid and yet weak. Keil holds that both contents and form put the authorship beyond doubt, sets out the structure as three gradually increasing strophes each beginning with praise and ending with the overthrow of the Egyptians, and reads the third verse of one who knows how to make war and has just proved himself the God who rules with unlimited might.

debates: When the song was composed: Ellicott and Keil both defend the traditional authorship from contents and form, Ellicott reporting that the prophetic statements in the later verses have led some to date it after Joshua and answering from the contrast between their vagueness and the definiteness of the narrative portion

How 'the Lord is a man of war' should be rendered: Clarke would change the English to the hero of the battle, since the phrase is now scarcely used except of ships of war, while Ellicott praises the translators for keeping the archaic boldness and dismisses the ancient softenings as turgid and weak
What the clause about preparing a habitation means: Ellicott reports two authorities for that rendering against a third with the Targums, the Greek, the Latin and most moderns for another
outliers: Calvin argues that the song confirms the history, since six hundred thousand men were made eye-witnesses of it and could have lied to nobody, no stranger being present
Wesley infers from the singing here that psalmody preceded the ceremonial law and so was not abolished with it
Gill reports a Jewish reckoning of ten songs beginning with one sung by Adam at the forgiveness of his sins
Ellicott observes that the song resembles Egyptian religious poetry, with which its author alone among Israelites of that time would have been familiar

4.pericope_label: Pharaoh’s host cast into the sea, and the blast of the Lord’s nostrils

schools.summary: Gill sees in the destruction an emblem of a later overthrow of antichrist, refers the right hand to Christ and calls its power the same as the Father's, identifies the blast of the nostrils with the wind and explains the figure, that it is as easily brought by God as a man's breath is drawn through his nostrils, and hears in the enemy's boast a man repenting that he had let the people go. Calvin explains why the narrative is told twice, that what had been plainly recounted is now set out in more glowing terms to assert that the drowning was manifestly God's work, and takes the comparison to stones and lead to mean that they were hurled by God's mighty hand into the deep and had no power to swim out.

Clarke observes that on such an expedition the principal nobility would have gone with their king, so that the overthrow reduced the country to the lowest extremity, and remarks how easily Israel might have gratified itself had the people been intent on plunder or their leader moved by ambition; he reduces the right hand to omnipotence manifested in a most extraordinary way, sets beside the passage a prophet's later recollection of the days of old and the leading of the people by the right hand of Moses, and identifies the blast of the nostrils with the strong east wind employed to dry the sea bed, here represented as the breath of God that congealed the waters. Wesley finds in the verb the force of casting an arrow out of a bow, reduces the phrase about excellency to great and excellent power, and reads the blast of the nostrils of the divine anger rather than of a wind, glossing the congealing as the depths standing still as though frozen.

Ellicott corrects two small points of tense in the opening verses, marks the end of the first strophe at the covering of the depths where the first historical review is complete, and thinks it probable that at that point Miriam and her chorus took up the opening refrain slightly modified and sang it; he calls the right hand a second anthropomorphism used here for the first time and corrects the following verbs as futures of continuance, and on the last verse finds a fact additional to the earlier narrative though in complete harmony with it, suggesting that as one wind had driven the waters back, a wind from the opposite quarter aided their return. Keil finds the point of the right hand in the timing, that the Lord overthrows his enemies at the very moment when they suppose themselves able to destroy his people, notices that the enemy's boast runs on in short clauses without a single connecting particle, which is what conveys his confidence, and states that one breath of God was enough to sink the proud foe.

debates: What the blast of the nostrils is: Clarke identifies it with the strong east wind that dried the sea bed and Gill explains the figure the same way, while Wesley reads it of the divine anger
outliers: Ellicott suggests that Miriam and her chorus took up the opening refrain at the close of each strophe, which would make the song a performance in parts
Ellicott finds in the last verse of the passage a fact additional to the prose narrative, a wind from the opposite quarter aiding the return of the waters
Clarke remarks how easily Israel might have enriched itself after the overthrow had the people been intent on plunder or their leader moved by ambition
Keil observes that the enemy's boast runs on in short clauses without a single connecting particle, and that this is what conveys his confidence

11.pericope_label: Who is like unto thee among the gods, and the nations that hear and tremble

schools.summary: Gill offers an alternative rendering that would make the comparison with the mighty ones, that is, the angels, and states plainly that everything from the middle of the passage to the close of the song is prophecy. Calvin attends to the form of the opening question, which breaks into exclamation because the grandeur of the subject transcends the power of words and expresses more than a plain assertion, marking admiration and assured confidence; on the tenses he grants that the Hebrew verb stands in the past but translates it as a future to make the sense clearer, since their hope for what was to come rested on mercies already received, and repeats at the next verse that he has not scrupled to change the tenses while adding that the past forms themselves confirm the certainty of the matter, a common figure with the prophets; and he grounds the boast on the strength named earlier.

Clarke recalls that the plagues appear to have been directed principally against the Egyptian gods, which were thereby confounded and made despicable; he thinks it very likely that an earthquake accompanied the overthrow, opening chasms in the sea bed, and finds it intimated in a psalm; he holds that the ode was dictated by the Spirit and that this verse and those to the end of the strophe are a prediction, so that several verbs would be better read as futures; and he notes that the rulers of the next people bore a title meaning heads or chiefs or captains. Wesley glosses the terms of the question one by one, the gods being so called only and meaning idols or princes, the holiness standing for justice and mercy and truth, and the fearfulness meaning that praise must be reverent; he supposes the dead bodies sank into the sands on which they were thrown and were sucked in, and finds a middle way on the tenses, that God had put them into the way to the promised place and would in due time bring them to the end of it.

Ellicott holds that the visitations were meant to show the Lord exalted far above all other gods and observes that the contrast is pressed by naming three points on which he is unapproachable, his holiness, his awefulness and his working of wonders; on the swallowing he sees no difficulty, since the sea that swallowed them is part of the earth, and uses the case to state a principle, that if we allow our common sense fair play and permit sacred writers the same latitude as profane ones we shall find wonderfully few discrepancies; he renders the verbs of the following verses as presents, since Hebrew wants a present tense and lets both preterite and future carry that force, and insists that the guidance was only just begun; and he takes the plural of the peoples to cover all the tribes of the desert and the land, points to the later histories for the fear actually felt, and notes that the inhabitants named are the Philistines, from whom the Holy Land afterwards took its name. Keil marks the opening verse as the beginning of the last strophe, where the song rises into firm assurance that the salvation begun will be finished, and supplies the philology of the titles.

debates: How the earth came to swallow them: Clarke supposes an earthquake opening chasms in the sea bed, Wesley that the bodies sank into the sands on which they were cast, and Ellicott that no explanation is needed since the sea is part of the earth

What tense the closing strophe carries: Clarke reads it as prediction and would render the verbs as futures, Calvin grants the Hebrew past and translates as future for clarity while allowing that the past form itself asserts certainty, and Ellicott renders throughout as present, since Hebrew wants a present tense
outliers: Ellicott states as a principle that if we allow our common sense fair play, and permit sacred writers the same latitude as profane ones, we shall find wonderfully few discrepancies
Clarke holds that the plagues were aimed principally at the gods of Egypt, so that the people are here exulting over them a second time
Calvin says the song breaks into exclamation because the grandeur of the subject transcends the power of words
Ellicott notes that the people named in the second clause are the Philistines, from whom the Holy Land afterwards took its name

17.pericope_label: Thou shalt plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance, and Miriam answers

schools.summary: Gill notes that the bringing in is ascribed to the Lord as much as the bringing out, refers the everlasting reign to Christ and dates its beginning in eternity, leaves it open whether the verse about Pharaoh's horse concludes the song by recapitulation or resumes the narrative, observes that the word for answering is masculine and that the women repeated the same song word for word after the men, and reports that Miriam's name, the same as Mary, signifies bitterness and is derived by the Hebrews from the bitterness of the times in which she was born. Calvin explains the figure of planting as denoting a firm habitation and finds a motive in the mention of the sanctuary, since by that commendation the desire of the land is excited in hearts otherwise indifferent; he judges that the verse about Pharaoh's horse is unsuited to the song and that the writer here returns to the history, rendering the verbs as pluperfects to avoid ambiguity; and he explains Miriam's part from the practice of the lyric poets, calling it the antistrophe, since God would have not only men proclaim the miracle but associated the women with them.

Clarke offers for the mountain either Canaan, a very mountainous country, or probably the hill on which the temple was afterwards built; he calls the closing line the grand chorus in which all the people joined, expressing dominion not only in the world but in the Church, not only under the law but under the Gospel, not only in time but through eternity, and offers a rendering of the phrase as for ever and onward; and he works out that Miriam was older than either of her brothers, since she was a girl able to manage the stratagem at the river when the younger was exposed and the elder was then barely three. Wesley argues that if God brought them out of Egypt he will bring them into Canaan, for having begun will he not make an end, adds that it is good dwelling where God dwells, and describes Miriam's part as a second assembly, the one leader giving out the psalm for the men and the other for the women with timbrels and dances after the usage of those times, recalling that famous victories were commonly applauded by the daughters of Israel.

Ellicott reports the view that one particular hill is intended and prefers to understand the land at large, which consists almost entirely of mountains and has only two plains of any extent, holds that the sanctuary can only mean the place where God was to put his name and notes that it is spoken of as already prepared; he judges that in simplicity, and in the force that comes of it, the closing line transcends all later expressions of the idea; he states flatly that the verse about Pharaoh's horse is parenthetic and forms no part of the poem, and accounts for it as an historical comment appended when the song was a separate document and kept when the records were gathered up; and on Miriam he says that in her we have the first of that long series of religious women in Scripture who are not merely pious but exercise a quasi-ministerial office, listing the later prophetesses and adding that the early Church had an order of deaconesses. Keil renders the promise as future and takes the singular horse to mean Pharaoh himself riding at the head of his army.

debates: What 'the mountain of thine inheritance' means: Clarke offers either Canaan at large or the temple hill, while Ellicott reports the view that one particular hill is intended and prefers the land at large

Whether the verse about Pharaoh's horse belongs to the song: Ellicott states flatly that it is parenthetic and no part of the poem and accounts for it as an appended historical comment, Calvin judges it unsuited and takes it as a return to the narrative with the verbs rendered as pluperfects, and Gill leaves the question open

How Miriam's singing relates to the men's: Calvin makes it the antistrophe of a lyric composition, Wesley a separate assembly of the women led by her, and Gill a verbatim repetition of what the men had sung
outliers: Ellicott makes Miriam the first of a series of women in Scripture who exercise a quasi-ministerial office, and connects the line with the later order of deaconesses
Clarke calculates that Miriam was older than both her brothers from her age at the exposure on the river
Gill reports that her name signifies bitterness and is derived by the Hebrews from the bitterness of the times in which she was born
Ellicott judges that in simplicity, and in the force that follows from it, the closing line transcends all later expressions of the same idea

22.pericope_label: From the Red Sea to the bitter waters of Marah

schools.summary: Gill reports two suppositions about the reluctance to leave the shore, that the people were intent on the spoil cast up on the beach, whose harness a rabbinic authority describes as ornamented with gold and silver and precious stones, or that they meant to turn back and take Egypt for themselves; he prefers the plain sense, that their general gave the word to march, and states the grievance at the bitter water simply, that they had been brought into a wilderness where they could find no water fit to drink. Calvin weighs the complaint and finds it inexcusable, since three days of thirst in a dry land was no light temptation and it is no wonder they groaned, but grief full of contumacy deserves no pardon; they should have turned their prayers to God, whereas they neglected to pray and violently assailed their leader, demanding of him the drink they knew God alone could give.

Henry adopts the difficulty of getting them away and adds that they were taken up with the sight or with the song or with the stripping of the dead bodies and did not care to go forward, drawing the lesson that the pleasures of the way to Canaan must not retard our progress but quicken it, though a wilderness lies ahead; he marks the trial that followed, that a want of water was a sore thing for young travellers and a diminution of their joy, by which God would train them up to difficulties.

Clarke places the wilderness they entered on the coast, on the road to the mountain, ascribes the murmuring to a state of great mental degradation brought on by long and oppressive bondage which had left them without firmness of character, and reports another traveller's conjecture identifying the site of the bitter spring with a place where a small rill still runs brackish unless diluted by dew or rain. Wesley gives the meaning of the name in three words.

Ellicott corrects the connecting word and marks the resumption of the narrative, noting that the people are carried two stages towards the mountain; he fixes the ground, that it is uncertain at what point of the coast they came out of the sea-bed though it can scarcely have been far from the modern port, and that the springs some seven miles from it, where there is considerable vegetation and a number of wells reckoned by different travellers at seven, seventeen and nineteen, may well have been the halting-place at which the song was composed and sung; he adds that the extreme bitterness of the springs at that end of the wilderness is attested by every traveller, that of the several such springs the most copious is scarcely the bitterest, and that the name means bitterness in both Hebrew and Arabic and appears to be a form of the root that gives the Latin words for the sea and for what is bitter. Keil turns to what was done there, that when the cry went up God showed a wood which took the bitterness away when thrown in, and observes that the Bedouins who know the country are acquainted with no such tree and with no other means of sweetening bitter water.

debates: Why the people had to be brought away from the shore: Gill reports that they were held by the spoil or by a design of returning to take Egypt and prefers the plain military sense, while Henry adopts the difficulty and adds the sight and the song and the stripping of the bodies

How the murmuring is to be judged: Calvin holds that grief full of contumacy deserves no pardon and that they should have prayed instead of assailing their leader, while Clarke excuses them by the mental degradation left by long bondage
outliers: Ellicott identifies a particular group of springs near the coast as the likely halting-place at which the song was composed and sung, and reports the wells there counted at seven, seventeen and nineteen by different travellers
Gill cites a rabbinic authority for the gold and silver and precious stones on the harness cast up from the sea
Keil observes that the Bedouins who know the country are acquainted with no tree that sweetens bitter water, and with no other means of doing it

25.pericope_label: The tree cast into the bitter waters, the statute, and the camp at the twelve wells

schools.summary: Calvin marks that Moses alone duly prayed while the people rose tumultuously against him, and that God might have given them sweet water at first but wished by the bitter to make prominent the bitterness which lurked in their hearts; he denies that the statute and ordinance refer to the whole law afterwards given on Sinai and makes them a special admonition, that if the Israelites were tractable and obedient God on his part would be kind and bountiful, with an implied rebuke that their troubles are brought on by their own sins, the Egyptians being the standing example of what he does to those who resist him; and he alone asks what the last station meant, that a more pleasant place was granted them but that this was a concession to their infirmity, because they had borne their thirst so impatiently. Gill says it is a happy thing to have a God to go to in a time of trouble, reads the statute as preparation for a body of laws since a people delivered from bondage were not to be without law to God, dates the arrival and cites Aben Ezra that they stayed only one day at the bitter waters, and reports two travellers' placements of the camp, taking the twelve wells and seventy palms at face value as plenty of water and shady trees, the fruit not being ripe at that season.

Clarke observes that Moses was not only their leader but also their mediator, reports that some think the tree was extremely bitter in itself, such as the quassia, and that God acted here as he generally does, correcting contraries by contraries, which among the ancient physicians was a favourite maxim; he holds that the following verse is precisely what the statute and ordinance intend, unfolding it into the acknowledgment of Jehovah alone with the avoidance of idolatry and the reception of his word as a divine revelation; and at the last stage he sets the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem, which make one well for each tribe and one palm for each of the seventy elders, against a traveller who found nine of the twelve wells and the other three choked with sand, and the palms multiplied into more than two thousand whose dates bring a considerable revenue to the Greek monks of the neighbouring port. Wesley draws the practical use, that it is the greatest relief of the cares of magistrates and ministers, when those under their charge make them uneasy, that they may have recourse to God by prayer, for he is the guide of the church's guides, and adds that God is to be acknowledged not only in creating things useful for man but in discovering their usefulness.

Ellicott takes a careful middle position on the tree: there are trees which have the power of sweetening bitter water, but none of them is at present found in the peninsula, and perhaps in ancient times there were forms of vegetable life there which do not now exist; Moses would scarcely have been shown a tree unless it had some virtue of its own, but on the other hand the tree alone is scarcely to be credited with the entire effect. He identifies the last camp with a particular valley where abundant grass grows thick and high and acacias and tamarisks are plentiful, and where, despite the ruthless denudation of the country by the Arabs, a certain number of palm-trees remain, though not seventy and either dwarf, that is trunkless, or otherwise stunted. Keil says only that the place has been sought from olden time in that same valley, about six miles south of the bitter spring.

debates: What the tree was and how it worked: Clarke reports the view that it was itself extremely bitter, God correcting contraries by contraries after the maxim of the ancient physicians, while Ellicott holds that the tree must have had some virtue of its own yet cannot be credited with the entire effect

What the statute and ordinance were: Clarke makes them the content of the following verse, Calvin a special admonition and not the law afterwards given on Sinai, and Gill a preparation for the body of laws to come

Whether the twelve wells and seventy palms were matched to the tribes and the elders, as Clarke reports from the Targums, or simply a well-watered camping ground, as Gill takes them and as the travellers cited by Clarke and Ellicott, who count neither twelve wells nor seventy palms, imply
outliers: Clarke cites a traveller who found nine of the twelve wells, the other three choked with sand, and the palms multiplied into more than two thousand, whose dates bring a considerable revenue to the Greek monks of the neighbouring port
Calvin holds that God might have given them sweet water at first but used the bitter to make prominent the bitterness which lurked in their hearts
